# Game design
<!-- Generated by scripts/generate_docs.py from scripts/templates/game-design.md. Edit the template. -->

Last Breath is a hold-and-spin game with no base game. A bet buys one dive, which is a complete hold-and-spin round on a board of five columns and three rows. The board starts empty. There are no reels, paylines or bonus to trigger, so the round you pay for is the whole game. The theme is deep-sea salvage: a coin is a cargo crate, a respin is a breath of oxygen, and the clock counts the breaths you have left.

I have built three dives, Classic, Drift and Tank. They all return about 96% of the bet in the long run, and they differ in how long a round lasts and how much it swings. The maths is in [math.md](math.md) and the exact figures are in [par-sheet.md](par-sheet.md). The numbers in this document are written by `scripts/generate_docs.py` from the config and the reports.

## How a round plays

A round starts with an empty board and the dive's starting clock. On each spin every empty cell draws once. It lands a crate with a small chance or stays empty. A crate that lands stays in its cell until the round ends. After the spin the dive's clock rule runs, and that rule is the only thing that sets the dives apart. The round ends when the board is full or the clock reaches zero. If the board fills, any breaths left are lost.

The award is the sum of the coins on the board, plus the Grand if the board is full. It is paid once, at the end of the round. The bet is chosen before the round and stays fixed. The bets are 0.20, 0.40, 1.00, 2.00, 4.00, 10.00 credits.

Money inside the game is a whole number of units, where one unit is a thousandth of the bet. It becomes credits only at settlement, as units times the bet divided by 1,000, in decimal arithmetic. The smallest coin is 0.05x the bet, every value is a multiple of it, and every bet is a multiple of 0.20 credits, so a payout is always a whole number of cents.

## Coins, jackpots and the Grand

A crate holds one coin. The coin is drawn from a weight table, and each dive uses one table. There are eight cash coins and three jackpot coins. A jackpot coin is an ordinary crate with a bigger face. It takes one cell and pays its face, and nothing ever doubles or boosts it.

| Coin or prize | Value, in bets | Value, in units |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Cash crate | 0.05x | 50 |
| Cash crate | 0.1x | 100 |
| Cash crate | 0.2x | 200 |
| Cash crate | 0.25x | 250 |
| Cash crate | 0.5x | 500 |
| Cash crate | 1x | 1,000 |
| Cash crate | 2x | 2,000 |
| Cash crate | 3x | 3,000 |
| Mini jackpot | 5x | 5,000 |
| Minor jackpot | 20x | 20,000 |
| Major jackpot | 100x | 100,000 |
| Grand | 1,000x | 1,000,000 |

The Grand is not a coin. It is a prize of 1,000 bets that is paid on top of the board when all 15 cells are full. No award can pass 5,000 bets, and the largest award that can happen is 2,500 bets in Classic and Tank and 1,300 in Drift, so the cap never applies. The weight tables are in [par-sheet.md](par-sheet.md).

## The three dives

**Classic Dive.** The clock starts at 3 breaths. Whenever at least one crate lands, the clock goes back to 3. A spin that lands nothing costs one breath, so the round ends after 3 dead spins in a row. Each crate is a relief because it refills the air. A round pays nothing in 21.03% of cases.

**Drift Dive.** The round is exactly 6 spins, and nothing that lands changes the count. The only way a round is shorter is a full board. It is the calm dive, because it almost always pays something, with a hit frequency of 99.95%, and it has the lowest standard deviation of the three. Its weight table has no Major, which keeps the big coins out of it. The config calls this dive `Static`, and the lab accepts both `static` and `drift`.

**Tank Dive.** The clock starts at 4 breaths and nothing refills it, so every spin costs one. Air tanks land in empty cells like crates but hold no coin. A tank adds 1, 2 or 3 breaths and clears from its cell in the same spin. A round takes at most 3 tanks, and a tank drawn after the third counts as nothing. A round is short, about 5.01 spins, and a tank that lands on the last breath can save it.

|  | Classic Dive | Drift Dive | Tank Dive |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| RTP, exact | 96.0019% | 96.0004% | 96.0004% |
| Standard deviation of a round, in bets | 6.29 | 1.54 | 4.41 |
| Hit frequency | 78.97% | 99.95% | 99.86% |
| Mean spins | 7.40 | 6.00 | 5.01 |
| Mean crates on the final board | 3.13 | 6.01 | 5.74 |
| Grand, 1 in | 32,541 | 904,262 | 65,370 |
| Reachable maximum, in bets | 2,500 | 1,300 | 2,500 |
| RTP, simulated, 10,000,000 rounds, seed 1 | 96.2052% | 96.0002% | 96.1743% |

Standard deviation orders the dives as Drift, Tank and Classic, from lowest to highest. The client labels them Low, Low to medium and Medium in that order.

## The Grand

A full board needs all 15 cells filled, and a cell fills only when a crate happens to land on it. The Grand comes about 1 round in 32,541 in Classic, 1 in 65,370 in Tank and 1 in 904,262 in Drift. It adds only 3.2%, 1.6% and 0.1% of the RTP, so it is a small part of the return. It is a large part of the swing. The term it adds to $E[A^2]$ is 75.8% of the total in Classic and 75.1% in Tank, against 33.7% in Drift, which is why Classic and Tank swing so much even though most rounds are small.

## Design notes

Boards are sparse by design. Every bet buys a whole round, so the round itself has to return about 96% of the bet. The average coin is worth 0.2970, 0.1595 and 0.1645 of the bet in the three dives, far below one bet, and a final board holds on average only 3.13, 6.01 and 5.74 crates out of 15 cells. Busy boards would pay far more than the bet. A hold-and-spin feature that follows a base game can afford busy boards, because it is only part of the return. Here it is all of it, so the chance that a cell fills is small.

The one number I tuned is each dive's crate chance. It is frozen at the integer, out of 1,000,000, that puts the exact RTP closest to 96%, and a test checks that no neighbouring integer is closer. The ladder, the shapes of the weight tables, the Grand, the clock rules and the tank limit are design choices that I made and did not derive.

A round starts on an empty board, so a round can pay nothing. That happens in 21.03% of Classic rounds, 0.05% of Drift rounds and 0.14% of Tank rounds. I chose this over placing starting coins on the board, because those coins would need a draw of their own, and that draw would be a hidden base game.

The tank limit is a rule and also a convenience for the maths. Without it a tank that adds one breath can leave a state unchanged, and the exact solve would need a linear system on an unbounded state space. [math.md](math.md) explains this under Tank.

## The client

The client is a demo with play money. It is a Blazor WebAssembly app that runs the same engine as the lab, in the browser, so every round is played locally with no server and nothing is paid out. I draw the crates, medals, bottles, wells and the mark as SVG from a script in `scripts/art/`, in one flat style. The dark and the light theme share one palette for everything drawn on the board, because the board is deep water in both themes, and differ in the page and in the plates. The air tank is a toon render made in Blender from a script kept in `scripts/art/blender/`. It ships as two small WebP files, one for each theme, because a bitmap cannot follow the theme colours through CSS, and the page loads only the one that matches the theme. The water behind the page is drawn the same way, and the art script keeps every tone of it dark or light enough for the page text to stay readable over it. Every cell of the board is a quiet recess, a well, and a coin that lands sits in it, so the board never changes shape. A tile shows only its value on a plate under the coin, and its label stays in its name and its tooltip, so the page says the same with or without the pictures. A player picks a dive and a bet, starts a round and watches the spins run by. A spin stays on the board for as long as what it held deserves: 450 milliseconds when nothing landed, 800 when crates landed, 1,300 when a jackpot landed and 1,100 on the last breath. The last breath is also marked by an amber edge round the board and a band over its top edge, and neither moves. On a wide screen the round is a stage that fills the window, with the board as large as the room allows and a side panel that lists every spin, newest first. The Skip key plays out the rest of a round, and the list shows what it played. When a round ends, a plate at the foot of the board shows the win and its multiple of the bet, says Big win for ten times the bet or more, and says how likely a result at least that good is. A win is put as how many dives in some number do at least that well, a round under the bet as how many dives in ten return less than the bet, and a round with nothing as how many dives surface with nothing. The figures come from the exact award distribution of the solver, which the page builds once for each dive, a few milliseconds of work, from the final crate probabilities in the report. The count of crates in a summary leaves jackpots out, which are counted on their own line. After the first round the side panel keeps a tally of the session: the rounds played, the total bet, the total returned and a strip of the last twelve results, in which ten times the bet fills the height and a round that returns nothing is a thin tick. The share returned so far appears from the tenth round, with the number of rounds it rests on, because a share of a few rounds says nothing. The page holds the tally in memory only and clears it with the balance. It sits next to the exact return of the dive from the reports, because a short session says little. The balance is play money and has a reset button. A jackpot that lands is marked on its card. A reduce-motion setting turns off the pop of a new tile, the count-up of the board total, the flying numbers and the bubbles behind the page, and it applies by itself when the system asks for reduced motion. Until the game has loaded, the page shows the mark, an empty board and one line, drawn in the page colours and not animated.

The dive cards and the Math panel read their figures from the reports when the site is built, so they show the numbers in [par-sheet.md](par-sheet.md). The Math panel also shows the seed of the most recent round, and `lab play --dive <dive> --seed <seed>` replays that round in the console. Opening the site with `?seed=<number>` makes the rounds repeatable, which the browser tests use.

The browser tests run in Chromium only, so I have not tested the client in any other browser. Free, Wreck and Crew are not built, and nothing in this repository computes them.
